name: To Kill a Mockingbird
blurb: Harper Lee's novel of a small Alabama town, a child narrator and a racially charged trial
title: To Kill a Mockingbird Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending
description: To Kill a Mockingbird summary: who Scout, Atticus, Tom Robinson and Boo Radley are, what happens at the trial, how it ends and what the title means.
h1: To Kill a Mockingbird: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: To Kill a Mockingbird is a 1960 novel by the American writer Harper Lee, awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1961. It is narrated by Scout Finch, who looks back on three years of her childhood in Maycomb, a fictional Alabama town during the Great Depression. Two threads run through it: the children's fascination with their unseen neighbor Boo Radley, and the trial of a Black man, Tom Robinson, whom Scout's father, the lawyer Atticus Finch, is appointed to defend.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: The narrator, a tomboyish girl who is six when the story begins
Scout's older brother, about four years her senior
Their widowed father, a lawyer and state legislator
The Finches' Black cook, who helps raise the children
A boy who spends summers in Maycomb and becomes the children's friend
A reclusive neighbor the children have never seen and tell rumors about
A Black farmhand accused of raping a white woman
A poor, violent white man and Mayella's father
Bob's eldest daughter, the accuser in the trial

body: Part One (chapters 1 to 11) covers roughly two years. Scout, Jem and their summer friend Dill turn the Radley house into a game, daring each other to touch it and acting out stories about Boo. Small gifts begin to appear in a knothole of a tree by the Radley property: chewing gum, coins, and two soap figures carved to look like Scout and Jem. Boo's brother Nathan then fills the hole with cement. On a winter night when their neighbor Miss Maudie's house burns, someone puts a blanket around Scout's shoulders without her noticing, and Jem realizes it was Boo.

Atticus is asked to defend Tom Robinson, and the town turns against the family. Scout fights classmates who insult her father. Atticus, who never boasts, surprises his children by shooting a rabid dog with a single shot. When Jem destroys the camellias of Mrs. Dubose, a bitter old neighbor, he is sentenced to read to her each afternoon; after her death Atticus explains that she was breaking a morphine addiction and calls her the bravest person he knew.

Part Two (chapters 12 to 31) centers on the trial. Calpurnia takes the children to her Black church. Atticus's sister Alexandra moves in to give Scout a more ladylike upbringing. The night before the trial, a mob comes to the jail to lynch Tom; Scout, not understanding the danger, chats with Mr. Cunningham, a farmer she knows, and the embarrassed men leave.

In court, the Ewells claim Tom beat and raped Mayella. Atticus shows that her injuries were on the right side of her face, that Bob Ewell writes with his left hand, and that Tom's left arm was crippled in a cotton gin accident as a boy. Tom testifies that Mayella invited him in and kissed him, and that her father saw it through the window. The evidence points to Bob having beaten his daughter, but the all-white jury convicts Tom. Jem is shattered. Soon afterward Tom is shot dead while trying to escape from a prison farm.

Bob Ewell, publicly humiliated, spits in Atticus's face and makes threats. On Halloween night, walking home in the dark from a school pageant where Scout played a ham, Jem and Scout are attacked. Jem's arm is broken. A man carries him home, and Scout realizes the stranger standing in Jem's bedroom is Boo Radley. Bob Ewell lies dead under a tree with a kitchen knife in his ribs.

At first Atticus assumes Jem killed Ewell in self-defense and insists the matter go before a court. Sheriff Tate refuses: he will report that Ewell fell on his own knife. Both men understand that Boo stabbed Ewell to save the children, and Tate argues that dragging a painfully shy man into the public eye for a good act would be its own wrong. Atticus accepts. Scout tells him that exposing Boo would be like shooting a mockingbird, picking up the lesson Atticus and Miss Maudie gave earlier: mockingbirds harm no one and only sing, so killing one is a sin.

Scout walks Boo home. Standing on his porch, she sees the street as he must have seen it for years, watching the children he quietly cared for. Boo goes inside and Scout never sees him again. The book ends with Atticus sitting by Jem's bed and Scout falling asleep.

The usual reading is that the title applies to two people. Tom Robinson is the mockingbird the town does kill, an innocent man destroyed by prejudice. Boo is the mockingbird the town decides to spare. Another common reading focuses on Scout's growth: the ending proves Atticus's advice that you never really understand someone until you consider things from their point of view. Some critics note a tension in the ending, since the law is bent to protect Boo after the law failed Tom; whether the cover-up is mercy or a second injustice is debated.

body.note: Harper Lee gave very few interviews about the book and did not publish an explanation of the ending.

ul: Racial injustice: Tom's conviction shows a legal system that fails a Black man even when the evidence clears him.
Moral courage: Atticus and Mrs. Dubose show that courage means doing the right thing when you know you will probably lose.
Innocence and growing up: Jem and Scout move from games about a scary neighbor to seeing real evil in adults.
Empathy: understanding Boo, Mayella and even the mob depends on imagining life from inside someone else's situation.
Class and social codes: Maycomb ranks its families by class and race, and the Ewells use the racial order to protect themselves.
Length: 31 chapters in two parts, about 280 to 320 pages depending on the edition.
Adaptations and related books: the 1962 film directed by Robert Mulligan with Gregory Peck as Atticus; Go Set a Watchman, an earlier draft published in 2015, follows an adult Scout.
Content advisory: frequent racial slurs, a rape accusation, a lynch mob, and a violent attack on children.
What teachers usually ask about: the meaning of the title, the adult Scout's narration looking back, Atticus as a moral model, and Boo Radley as a symbol of the town's fear of difference.

check.q: What evidence suggests Tom Robinson did not beat Mayella?
options: A witness saw him at work in another town
Her injuries were on the right side and his left arm is useless
check.why: Atticus shows Mayella was hit by a left-handed attacker, which Tom, with a crippled left arm, could not be, while Bob Ewell writes with his left hand.

check.q: Who saves Jem and Scout from Bob Ewell?
check.why: Boo Radley fights off Ewell, stabs him and carries the injured Jem home.

check.q: What does Sheriff Tate decide to report about Bob Ewell's death?
options: That Jem killed him in self-defense
That Ewell fell on his own knife
check.why: Tate says Ewell fell on his knife so that Boo is not dragged into public view.

faq.q: Why is the book called To Kill a Mockingbird?
faq.a: Atticus tells his children it is a sin to kill a mockingbird, and Miss Maudie explains that the birds only make music and harm no one. The image points to innocent people hurt by others, chiefly Tom Robinson and Boo Radley.
After his conviction, Tom is shot and killed by guards while trying to escape from a prison farm, before his appeal can be heard.

faq.q: How old is Scout in To Kill a Mockingbird?
faq.a: Scout is six when the story begins in 1933 and about eight at the end; the story is told by Scout as an adult looking back.
